concepts.gloss: An occasion of spoken or written expression with a time, place, speaker/writer, and addressee.
Time interpreted relative to the utterance act or an available shifted perspective.
Place interpreted in relation to utterance location or relative proximity.
Interpretation of first/second-person forms from the roles of speaker and addressee.
Systematic interpretation through utterance-act parameters, unlike ordinary variation in proper-name reference.
Location specified by named places or non-utterance reference events.
Whole phrase or word whose referent is identified through deixis.
Item encoding deictic information, possibly within a larger deictic expression.
Pointing, gaze, touch or graphic mark used to clarify deictic reference.
Perspective from which deictic reference is interpreted, ordinarily the current speaker.
Default reading of deictic expressions from a speaker/writer perspective.
Interpretation of a notice from its current reader's temporal perspective.
Deictic perspective transferred to a reader or represented thinker in particular contexts.

rules.statement: Deictic reference shifts systematically with the time, place or participants of an utterance-act; a proper name may vary in reference without having such a deictic meaning.
rules.condition: When interpreting I, now, here, this or that, identify the relevant utterance-act anchor; contrast with a proper name whose choice of bearer is context-dependent but not systematically anchored to utterance roles.

contrast.text: A says, 'I will call tomorrow.' [I refers to A]
B says, 'I will call tomorrow.' [I refers to B]
A says, 'Casey called.' [the proper name is not deictic]
B says, 'Casey called.' [a different Casey may be intended]

rules.concept: deictic and non-deictic spatial and temporal location
rules.statement: Time and place may be located deictically relative to an utterance-act or non-deictically relative to a named place or independently identified event.
rules.condition: Classify here and last week as utterance-relative when so used; distinguish explicit place-names and times measured from independently established events, which do not acquire deictic status merely by varying in reference.

contrast.text: Our courier works here. [utterance-relative place]
Our courier works in Bristol. [named non-deictic place]
We arrived last Friday. [deictic time]
We arrived the Friday after the conference. [non-deictic time]

rules.statement: A deictic expression is the whole utterance-anchored referring constituent; its deictic marker is the word that encodes this property, which may be a proper part of the expression or the entire expression.
rules.condition: In those blue folders, treat the NP as the expression and those as its marker; in last month, last is the marker; with a stand-alone item such as here, marker and expression coincide.

contrast.text: Put those blue folders away. [those = marker, whole NP = expression]
We met last month. [last = marker, last month = expression]
Please stand here. [here = marker and expression]
I can reach this. [this = marker and expression]

rules.statement: Pointing, gaze, touch and diagrammatic marks can identify deictic referents and cooperate with nominal descriptions; gestures are sometimes necessary but are not universally required.
rules.condition: Where here, there, this, that or another locally dependent form is ambiguous among visible alternatives, examine accompanying gesture, eye contact or diagram arrows; when the context is clear, no special indexing act need be present.

contrast.text: [Pointing at a shelf] Place the parcel there. [gesture identifies place]
[Pointing among red binders] Please pass that red binder. [gesture and words cooperate]
[Beside the only door] Wait here. [no explicit gesture needed]
[Arrow on a printed map] Our cabin is here. [diagrammatic index]

rules.statement: The deictic centre is ordinarily the speaker or writer and changes between speakers; expressions written in a personal message may be anchored to the time of writing rather than reading.
rules.condition: Interpret first-person, local and temporal deictics by default from the current utterer's perspective and recalculate that anchor after a conversational speaker change, subject to specially shifted-centre uses.

exceptions.description: Deictic interpretation can shift from the speaker/writer to a reader of a standing notice or a represented thinker's viewpoint, as the same subsection expressly notes.

contrast.text: A: 'I am sitting here.' [I/here anchored to A]
B: 'I am sitting here too.' [I/here anchored to B]
In a letter: 'I began this draft two hours ago.' [writer's time]
'This cup is warmer than that one.' [proximity assessed from speaker]
[Notice] 'Now submit your ticket.' [now shifts to each reader's time rather than the writer's]

rules.concept: reader-centred deixis in standing written notices
rules.statement: A standing written notice can anchor now to the time each addressee reads it, rather than to the author's writing time.
rules.condition: When the utterance is a notice addressed to successive readers, interpret an instruction's now relative to the reader's occasion of reading or action; do not extend this to all written occurrences of now.

contrast.text: [Sign beside sink] 'Now rinse your hands.' [reader's time]
[A different reader encounters the sign later] 'Now rinse your hands.' [time shifts]
[Letter] 'I am writing now.' [writer's time, contrasting context]

rules.statement: Temporal expressions in reports of another person's thoughts may be anchored to the reported person's perspective rather than to the actual utterance; both readings can be possible.
rules.condition: In Mina realised the guests had left two days ago, allow ago to locate an interval before Mina's realisation or before the current speaker's utterance, without treating shifted interpretation as obligatory.

contrast.text: Mina realised the guests had left two days ago. [possible Mina-centred reading]
Mina realised the guests had left two days ago. [possible speaker-centred reading]
The investigator thought the parcel had arrived a week ago. [reported viewpoint may anchor ago]
The parcel arrived a week ago. [normal utterance-centred reference]
